name: Planning Together
title: Planning Together
answer: Planning together means teachers on a team use AI to draft shared materials, then review and revise them as a group. It matters because it cuts duplicated work and turns planning meetings into time for teachers to learn from each other. The team, not the tool, still decides what the curriculum covers.

sections.body: Professional learning communities already give teachers time to share lessons, study student work, and solve problems, and this idea is about making that time more productive with AI. Instead of every teacher on a grade level team planning the same unit alone, the team divides the unit, drafts pieces with AI, and reviews each other's work. Shared drafts reduce duplicated effort, since separate AI planning sessions repeat the same hours of work. The review step is where the real learning happens, because teachers examine and improve each other's materials. A related use is the standards audit, where AI compares unit plans against the state standards and flags what looks missing or lightly covered.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a grade level team might ask AI to draft a common assessment and then spend its meeting revising that draft together rather than building it from scratch. For a shared unit, the team splits the work, has AI draft each part, and then reviews one another's sections so the whole team owns the result. Teams can also run a standards audit by having AI compare their set of unit plans against the state standards and flag standards that appear missing or only lightly addressed. The team then checks each flag by hand, because tools can misread how a standard is actually addressed in a lesson. The audit results guide revisions for the following year. The text does not give separate grade band examples.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. Its claims rest on practice and on what professional learning communities commonly do, such as sharing lessons, studying student work, and solving problems together. The book states that teachers who plan together often plan better and that teams using shared AI drafts save time and improve quality, but it presents these as practical observations rather than research findings. The standards audit is likewise described as a working method, with the caution that tools can misread standards. So this idea should be treated as practice based rather than research proven.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that AI drafts are starting points, not finished materials, and the team must review them before use. In the standards audit, the team has to check every flag because a tool can misread how a standard is addressed, so the audit guides revisions rather than dictating them. Decisions about what the curriculum covers and what gets taught stay with the teachers, not the tool. The text does not set out further rules, products, or legal requirements, and nothing here is legal advice.
